result.question: I need to know whether the fault in Transformer 1 at MAIN is getting worse or changing character. Run a DGA fault classification on the first and the last complete oil sample between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene. Tell me each sample's fault class and confidence. Then tell me whether the class moved toward a higher-energy or higher-temperature fault, for example PD to D1, or T1 to T2/T3. If the two classifications disagree, explain which one you trust more and why, based on the absolute gas levels and not just the ratios. Then recommend one specific next check, such as a confirmatory resample, an OLTC compartment sample or an electrical test. Count a sample as complete only if all five gases are non-null. If there is only one complete sample in the window, classify that one alone and say that no progression can be judged.
result.answer:
The `interpret_dga` tool is down ("LLM unavailable" on two attempts), so I classified both samples manually using the IEC 60599 three-ratio method, cross-checked with Duval Triangle 1. No further data is needed — all inputs are already in hand.

## Samples used (all 4 in window are complete; first and last taken)

| Sample | H2 | CH4 | C2H6 | C2H4 | C2H2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **2024-01-15** (first) | 2845 | 7406 | 5467 | 16684 | 7 |
| **2024-01-18** (last) | 2900 | 7350 | 5450 | 16600 | 7 |

## Classification

**Sample 1 (2024-01-15)**
- C2H2/C2H4 = 0.0004 · CH4/H2 = 2.60 · C2H4/C2H6 = 3.05
- IEC 60599 ratio class: **T2 (thermal fault, 300–700 °C)** — borderline to T3 (C2H4/C2H6 ratio 3.05 sits between the Rogers >3 and IEC 2015 >4 thresholds for T3)
- Duval Triangle 1: 30.7 % CH4 / 69.2 % C2H4 / 0.03 % C2H2 → **T3 (>700 °C)**
- Confidence: **high** that it is a thermal fault (no arcing signature); **moderate** on T2 vs T3

**Sample 2 (2024-01-18)**
- C2H2/C2H4 = 0.0004 · CH4/H2 = 2.53 · C2H4/C2H6 = 3.05
- IEC 60599 ratio class: **T2**, same borderline position
- Duval Triangle 1: 30.7 % / 69.3 % / 0.03 % → **T3**
- Confidence: same as Sample 1

## Is it progressing?

**No — the fault class has not moved and the gases are flat.** Every gas changed by ≤ 2 % over the three days (H2 +55, CH4 −56, C2H6 −17, C2H4 −84, C2H2 0), all well inside lab repeatability. Acetylene stayed at 7 ppm, so there is no drift toward D1/D2 (arcing), and the ratios did not shift toward a hotter thermal class. Character is unchanged.

## Which classification to trust

The two *samples* agree with each other. The disagreement is between *methods*: IEC ratios say T2, Duval says T3. **I trust T3.** The absolute levels settle it: ethylene at ~16,600 ppm is roughly 100× the IEC 60599 90th-percentile typical value, and ethylene is the dominant gas (69 % of the hydrocarbon triangle). Ethylene dominance is the hallmark of metal hot-spotting above 700 °C; a genuine T2 fault would be methane/ethane-led with ethylene as a minority gas. The IEC ratio only lands on T2 because C2H4/C2H6 (3.05) is just short of the 4.0 boundary, and that ratio is diluted by an ethane level that is itself enormous. The near-zero acetylene also rules out OLTC-contamination as the source — an OLTC leak would bring acetylene with it.

Note also that with gases this high and flat, the fault may already be a mature, quasi-steady hot spot rather than an accelerating one — but "not getting worse over 3 days" at these concentrations is not reassuring; these levels are in the range where IEEE C57.104 Condition 4 applies.

## Recommended next check

**Confirmatory resample now (same sampling point, same syringe/lab procedure, accredited lab), with CO, CO₂ and furan (2‑FAL) added to the analysis.** Purpose: (1) rule out a sampling or lab artefact producing 16,000 ppm ethylene before you make an outage decision, and (2) the CO₂/CO ratio and furans tell you whether the >700 °C hot spot involves cellulose (winding/lead insulation) or is bare-metal only (core, clamp, tank circulating current). If the resample confirms the levels, plan a de-energized winding resistance and core-ground insulation test, and treat the unit as a candidate for removal from service pending those results.
